UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                           )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                )                   Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                           )



                 ANSWER AND MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER
                OF THE INDEPENDENT MARKET MONITOR FOR PJM

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules and Regulations, 1

Monitoring Analytics, LLC, acting in its capacity as the Independent Market Monitor

(“Market Monitor”) for PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), 2 submits this answer to, and

moves for leave to answer, the answer submitted by PJM on September 23, 2026

(“September 23rd Answer”), and to the answer submitted by the Data Center Coalition 3

(“DCC”) to the September 23rd Answer on October 1, 2026.

       On August 13, 2026, PJM submitted a proposal “to establish Interim Resource

Adequacy Service (“IRAS”)—a service to be implemented by PJM solely during periods

when there are insufficient resources to reliably meet demand in real time operations”

(“IRAS Filing”). 4 The IRAS rules would (id.) “enable PJM to prioritize load reduction in

2    Capitalized terms used herein and not otherwise defined have the meaning used in the PJM Open
     Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”), the PJM Operating Agreement (“OA”) or the PJM Reliability
     Assurance Agreement (“RAA”).

     <https://www.datacentercoalition.org/members>.

     Affidavit”).
 zones/areas where New Large Loads [citation omitted] have not brought their own new

capacity or had their capacity needs covered through the Reliability Backstop Procurement

(“RBP”).” An order on the RBP auction process issued September 29, 2026 (“RBP Order”). 5

       The IRAS Filing has not been supported as just and reasonable. The IRAS Filing is

not just and reasonable and it should be rejected. The IRAS Filing proposal for curtailments

is not actually a proposal but is rather an attempt to shift responsibility for curtailments to

the states. To the extent that the IRAS Filing would create actual rules, it has not been

demonstrated to be consistent with cost causation principles, the same defect in the RBP

Filing identified in the RBP Order (at PP 150–157). The IRAS Filing is unjust and

unreasonable, and attempting to implement it will damage PJM markets and create

unintended consequences. Contrary to DCC’s argument that the IRAS Filing proposes rules

that exceed the Commission’s jurisdiction, the IRAS Filing’s core flaw is the failure to

provide a solution that is consistent with federal jurisdiction, that is consistent with cost

causation principles and that is consistent with federal policy.

       The IRAS Filing is PJM’s non responsive response to broad agreement among policy

makers, regulators, and developers, captured in the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and

Principles, on the need to ensure that data centers bring their own new generation and pay

their own way and to prioritize the protection of reliability and affordability for all the

other customers. 6    7   The Pledge affirms: “The Ratepayer Protection Pledge and the




5    See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 196 FERC ¶ 61,245 (“RBP Order”).

     <https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/?utm_source=wh_social
     _share_button>, Proclamation No. 11014, 91 Fed. Reg. 11439 (Mar. 4, 2026) (“Today, pursuant to the
     Ratepayer Protection Pledge, leading United States hyperscalers and AI companies guarantee that
     data centers’ energy needs will not increase household electricity costs for American citizens.
     Instead, these companies will build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity
     needed to satisfy their energy demands, and pay for all new power delivery infrastructure
     upgrades to service their data centers. They will voluntarily negotiate new, separate rate structures
     with their utilities and relevant State governments, and pay those rates, and for their infrastructure,


                                                   -2-
 commitments embodied therein effectuate the national policy of the United States.” The

Commission has recognized the Pledge and Principles.8 The Pledge and Principles should

guide the development of rules to support resource adequacy by requiring data centers to

bring their own new generation, or when that is not done, procuring new capacity to serve




     whether they use the electricity or not. They will also invest in local communities and coordinate
     with grid operators to contribute to a more reliable grid.”) (“Pledge”). On July 23, 2026, over 200
     additional entities joined the pledge. See The White House, “President Trump’s Ratepayer
     Protection Pledge Secures American AI Dominance, Protects Consumers” (July 23, 2026),
     <https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/07/president-trumps-ratepayer-protection-pledge-secures-
     american-ai-dominance-protects-consumers/?utm_source=wh_social_share_button>.

     <https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm> (“Principles”). Two principles
     apply to the contemplated procurement of new generation. First, the procurement should
     “[p]rovide 15-year price certainty for new capacity resources” [emphasis]. The statement notes that
     this can be done in through a “Reliability Backstop Auction,” but does not require that this auction
     be a centralized procurement by PJM or that PJM customers assume risks. Second, “PJM should
     allocate the cost of any new capacity through the aforementioned Reliability Backstop Auction to
     load serving entities (LSEs) with new data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or
     agreed to be curtailable.” The principles, agreed to by the Governors of PJM States Indiana, Ohio,
     Maryland Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia, Delaware, Illinois, Michigan, New Jersey,
     Tennessee, North Carolina and Kentucky, call for PJM to do the allocation and to match data
     centers to the costs not excluding risks of new resources or commitments to curtail. Additional
     principles that going beyond the RBF Proposal, the Market Proposal, or potential alternatives,
     include: (i) extending the price collar for two additional RPM Base Residual Auctions, (ii) PJM
     improving load forecasting, (iii) accelerating generator interconnections, i.e., the Reliability
     Resource Initiative (RRI), and (iv) continued efforts to reform the capacity market.

8    See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211 at PP 2, 5, 8, 32 & 69 (2026) (“Large Load Show
     Cause Order”). The Large Loads Show Cause Order states (at P 66) (“We next preliminarily find
     that PJM’s Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks adequate mechanisms to
     mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers, which may result in unjust and
     unreasonable rates for transmission service. In particular, we are concerned about the apparent lack
     of: (1) transparency regarding the assignment of Network Upgrades, and their associated costs, that
     are needed to provide transmission service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads; and (2) a
     pro forma cost recovery agreement between PJM, the relevant transmission owner, and the Eligible
     Customer taking transmission service on behalf of large loads that help ensure that Eligible
     Customers bear the risk and are ultimately responsible for costs incurred to provide transmission
     service, including the cost of Network Upgrades.”).



                                                 -3-
 data centers and ensuring that data centers pay for that capacity and that those costs are not

assigned, allocated or otherwise imposed on other customers.

          The IRAS Filing ignores the Pledge and Principles. The IRAS Filing is a convoluted,

inconsistent, confusing proposal that PJM justifies based on a misreading of jurisdictional

responsibilities and under which PJM denies responsibility for reliability and assigns key

undefined and inappropriate roles to the states. The September 23rd Answer does not

answer the objections raised and does not provide the support needed to approve the IRAS

Filing.

          In addition to rejecting the IRAS Filing as not just and reasonable, an order should

be issued, finding that the existing rules relating to resource adequacy for serving data

centers in the PJM Region are unjust and unreasonable under Section 206 of the Federal

Power Act. Such an order should direct that PJM file rules for the PJM Region establishing

tariff defined curtailment obligations for wholesale service to data centers during a defined,

limited transition period that would allow data centers that interconnect without new

generation the time to contract for new generation but that would include curtailment rules

as a long term solution to meeting the need for data centers to bring their own new

generation.

          These requirements meet the goals of the Pledge and Principles and can be

implemented immediately.

I. ANSWER

          A. Neither the IRAS Filing nor the Market Monitor’s Proposed Remedial
             Directive Unduly Discriminates Against Data Centers.

          The RBP Filing reveals PJM’s confusion on the purpose of the RBP Filing and, by

implication, the purpose of the associated IRAS Filing. 9 The RBP Order directs PJM to file




9    Cf. PJM Answer, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (September 10, 2026) at 64 (“It is fallacious to suggest
     that a just and reasonable cost allocation approach must either identify specific loads (which are


                                                -4-
 additional rules to address the central issue, to assign RBP auctions costs (at PP 150–157),

finding “PJM has not adequately demonstrated that its proposal is just and reasonable and

consistent with the cost causation principle.” Market Monitor believes that this means that

the costs of serving data centers should be assigned to data centers. Assigning the RBP

auction costs to data centers meets the definition of the cost causation standard because

data centers are the cause of the problem to be solved by the RBP Filing. The stated purpose

of the IRAS Filing is to define rules that would require curtailments when some data centers

fail to bring their own new generation. Yet the IRAS Filing fails to meet its stated purpose.

       The Commission’s issuance of Remedial Directives advocated by the Market

Monitor would solve the problem in a manner fully consistent with both cost causation

principles and the Pledge and Principles. 10

       DCC, nevertheless, argues (at 18) “PJM has not demonstrated that New Large Loads

are in fact causing PJM’s capacity shortfall.” DCC also argues (at 16–19) that the “factual

differences” relied upon by PJM are not adequate to justify discriminatory treatment.

DCC’s surprising assertion that the reasons for the IRAS Filing do not justify rules specific

to data centers has no merit. It is data centers that are uniquely seeking interconnection at

the scale and at the speed sought by data centers. It is clear from the evidence that data




     not FPA-jurisdictional actors) and not the LSEs serving those loads or be limited to one type of load
     when the resource adequacy shortfall is caused by all types of loads that comprise the subject Load
     Adjustments” [emphasis in original].); RBP Filing, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (August 13, 2026) at 1
     (PJM proposes “to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”)—a one-time
     procurement of new capacity to address resource adequacy challenges in the PJM Region arising
     from insufficient commitments of capacity in the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Reliability Pricing Model
     (“RPM”) Auctions, primarily driven by the unprecedented addition of large loads, most notably
     data centers”).

10   See Protest of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (August 21,
     2026) at 28–32; Protest of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Docket No. ER26-3515-000
     (September 3, 2026) (“IMM Protest”) at 36–40.



                                                  -5-
 center customers are uniquely the cause of the reliability issues faced by PJM. 11 It is

uniquely data center customers that are seeking to rely on curtailments so that they can

participate in the wholesale power markets before the infrastructure needed to serve them

is ready.

       The Pledge and Principles demonstrate that data centers recognize that the data

centers are causing the problems that the IRAS Filing purports to address and that the data

centers recognize that they need to bring their own generation and pay their own costs.

DCC never mentions the Pledge and Principles, and the DCC fails to explain how its

opposition comports with the Pledge and Principles and the commitments and public

positions of some of the most significant members of the DCC. DCC’s arguments that the

IRAS Filing fails because it is unduly discriminatory are not supported and should be

rejected.

       B. PJM Can File a Complete Proposal Consistent with the Pledge and Principles
          for the Same Reasons It Defends the Commission’s Jurisdiction to Approve
          the IRAS Filing.

       The September 23rd Answer defends (passim) against protests and comments alleging

the IRAS Filing proposes rules beyond the Commission’s jurisdiction to approve. PJM is

correct that the IRAS Filing is within the Commission’s jurisdiction to approve. In addition,

for the same reasons that PJM provides in defense of the IRAS Filing, PJM could have

proposed rules that recognize the scope of the Commission’s jurisdiction and that therefore

actually address the issue affecting wholesale energy markets and regional reliability

consistent with the Pledge and Principles.




11   The      most     recent     Base      Residual     Auction      Reports       are   located at
     <https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/reports/Reports/2026.shtml>. Also see, the 2026 Quarterly
     State     of   the      Market      Report     for    PJM:     January       through    June at
     <https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/reports/PJM_State_of_the_Market/2026.shtml>.



                                               -6-
        The IRAS Filing falls far short of what is needed because PJM fails to propose

curtailment rules that are consistent with the Commission’s jurisdiction and therefore have

the intended result. Instead, PJM relies on speculation about what states may do to

complete its proposal. The IRAS Filing should be rejected because it does not result in

assigning the costs and risks of meeting data center load to data center customers. PJM

failed to file a consistent regional solution consistent with its role as an RTO and consistent

with the Commission’s jurisdiction. PJM’s balkanized approach cannot create a consistent

regional market that applies the same rules across the entire market and that does not create

unintended consequences across states that result from different interpretations of

curtailment rules. PJM’s approach is likely to create more problems than it solves because it

fails to include a comprehensive and consistent regional approach.

       PJM attempts to justify its incomplete IRAS Filing based on an incorrect statement of

the Commission’s jurisdiction. States have jurisdiction over generation in their own states

and over retail sales in their own states. States do not have jurisdiction over neighboring

states. States cooperating with (or failing to cooperate with) other states to regulate

interstate commerce, displacing federal regulation, is not cooperative federalism. PJM

should not attempt to transfer its responsibility to operate the regional capacity market to

the states. The Supreme Court has recognized that the Commission’s jurisdiction extends to

rules related to retail customers’ participation in the wholesale power markets as sellers. 12




12   See FERC v. EPSA, 577 U.S. 260, 281 (2016) (EPSA) (“Yet a FERC regulation does not run afoul of
     §824(b)’s proscription just because it affects—even substantially—the quantity or terms of retail
     sales. It is a fact of economic life that the wholesale and retail markets in electricity, as in every
     other known product, are not hermetically sealed from each other. To the contrary, transactions
     that occur on the wholesale market have natural consequences at the retail level. And so too, of
     necessity, will FERC’s regulation of those wholesale matters. Cf. Oneok, Inc. v. Learjet, Inc., 575 U. S.
     373, 387… (2015) (noting that in the similarly structured world of natural gas regulation, a “Platonic
     ideal” of strict separation between federal and state realms cannot exist). When FERC sets a
     wholesale rate, when it changes wholesale market rules, when it allocates electricity as between
     wholesale purchasers—in short, when it takes virtually any action respecting wholesale


                                                   -7-
 The Supreme Court recognizes federal jurisdiction over the terms and conditions of retail

customers’ participation in wholesale markets even as they remain retail customers.

       PJM apparently believes, and DCC argues (at 12–15), that because data centers are

retail customers, PJM cannot require that the load serving entities (“LSEs”) who serve them

place terms and conditions on service to data centers. 13 PJM has not reconciled this position

with the jurisdiction currently exercised under the Reliability Assurance Agreement

(“RAA”). The RAA requires LSEs to meet their obligations, defined in the RAA, from

capacity provided by generators that meet the terms and conditions of the RAA. 14 LSEs are

not permitted under the RAA to rely on Generation Capacity Resources that do not meet

these terms and conditions regardless of state views about the capability of the facilities. 15

Resources included in Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”) Plans under Schedule 8.1 to the

RAA must also meet requirements specified in the RAA. 16

       PJM does not explain why it cannot propose to require terms and conditions for the

capacity required to meet data center loads through the LSEs that serve them when it can

and does include terms and conditions through LSEs on the capacity that can meet the

reliability obligations of LSEs.




     transactions—it has some effect, in either the short or the long term, on retail rates. That is of no
     legal consequence.”).

13   See RBP Filing at 64 (“It is fallacious to suggest that a just and reasonable cost allocation approach
     must … identify specific loads (which are not FPA-jurisdictional actors) …”).

14   See RAA Schedules 9, et seq. & 10 (rules for PJM to evaluate capability and deliverability of
     Generation Resources).

15   See id.

16   See RAA § 7.2.

        DCC objects that data centers are retail customers, and that requirements related to

curtailments affect their consumption at retail. 17 The IRAS Filing is not about retail power

use. Any curtailments directed by PJM support the reliable operation of the wholesale

market and power grid. PJM does not operate retail markets or local infrastructure. IRAS

curtailments are for the sole purpose of protecting wholesale market reliability by curtailing

customers that have not procured through their LSEs the necessary capacity in the

wholesale market. The focus of the IRAS Filing is regional resource adequacy and the

regional capacity markets. An attempt by a state to regulate such matters would unlawfully

intrude on an area subject to federal jurisdiction and would be preempted. 18

       PJM’s attempt to manufacture unneeded and inappropriate state involvement in

operating the wholesale energy markets confuses rather than clarifies the jurisdictional

boundaries. Allowing states to perform the role proposed in the IRAS Filing (and the

allocation function in the RBP Filing) 19 is, under Hughes, an abdication of the RTO’s

responsibility under federal law. 20

       The case for federal jurisdiction is stronger in the IRAS case than it was in EPSA. The

IRAS case concerns the consequences of the failure to procure capacity under proposed

capacity market rules. The IRAS Filing should provide rules for curtailment that are a




17   See DCC at 8 (“IRAS seeks to prescribe resource procurement and curtailment requirements for
     retail customers within the PJM region.”).

18   See Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 163 (2016) (“We agree with the Fourth
     Circuit’s judgment that Maryland’s program sets an interstate wholesale rate, contravening the
     FPA’s division of authority between state and federal regulators. As earlier recounted, … the FPA
     allocates to FERC exclusive jurisdiction over ’rates and charges . . . received . . . for or in connection
     with’ interstate wholesale sales. §824d(a). Exercising this authority, FERC has approved the PJM
     capacity auction as the sole rate setting mechanism for sales of capacity to PJM, and has deemed
     the clearing price per se just and reasonable”).

19   See RBP Order at PP 150–157.

20   See id.



                                                    -9-
 condition of taking wholesale service when the data center load has not procured capacity

required for it to be served reliably. The purpose of the IRAS is to address the particular

and extraordinary demands related to resource adequacy and the capacity market

attributable to the rapid interconnection of data centers in the PJM Region. The Supreme

Court held that the Commission has preempted state action related to the capacity market

rules.21 Data centers are receiving wholesale sales along with the associated terms and

conditions of such sales from PJM through Load Serving Entities.

       PJM’s attempt to justify its incomplete proposal based on an incorrect jurisdictional

analysis and to instead rely on speculation about actions that states may take is insufficient

to support the IRAS Filing as just and reasonable. For all these reasons, PJM’s approach is

unjust and unreasonable. The IRAS Filing should be rejected for that reason.

       C. The IRAS Filing Has Not Been Shown to be Just and Reasonable.

       PJM’s Answer ignores or fails to adequately address the issues raised by the Market

Monitor. These issues include: PJM’s failure to support its policy of interconnecting new

large loads when there is not capacity to serve them; PJM’s failure to include the locational

constraints that are an essential feature of PJM’s capacity market; PJM’s failure to

appropriately or consistently define the capacity that can meet the data center obligation to

bring their own new capacity; PJM’s unjust shifting of ELCC risk to other customers; and

PJM’s failure to support its definition of large load; PJM’s proposal to interrupt IRAS

customers who paid for capacity before demand side resources who sold capacity.

               1. PJM Fails to Justify Its Failure to Recognize Locational Constraints.

       Locational constraints are core to the PJM capacity market construct. PJM failed to

address the concerns raised by the stakeholders about the lack of locational constraints in




21   See 578 U.S. 150, 163.



                                            - 10 -
 the RBP and IRAS Filings. 22 Modeling locational constraints in the capacity market is

essential. Rules that ignore and exclude locational constraints cannot ensure reliability,

cannot incent investors to site new generation where it is most needed, and do not protect

existing customers from the increased costs caused by data center load. The RBP and IRAS

Filings do not accomplish PJM’s two central stated objectives: provide reliability and

protect customers from increased costs related to data centers.23

       PJM argues that locational constraints should be ignored for two reasons: PJM

cannot accurately predict transmission topography 15 years into the future; and PJM’s

deliverability analysis at the time of unit interconnection is a substitute for the CETO/CETL

analysis. Neither argument is correct or supportable.

       The fact that PJM cannot accurately predict transmission topography 15 years in

advance is not an excuse for ignoring the core locational feature of the capacity market.

Requiring that the generation be located electrically close to the data center load would be a

reasonable approach that would resolve the basic issue. PJM ignores that option.

       PJM repeated the clearly incorrect and unsupported argument that the deliverability

test required of all capacity resources means that “there does not need to be any locational

requirement for BYONC.” 24 If PJM’s argument were correct, there would never be a need

for the LDA CETO/CETL analysis. Of course, PJM conducts the CETO and CETL analysis to

ensure that, for each LDA, the sum of the internal capacity in each LDA and the ability to

import capacity is enough to meet the reliability criterion for each modeled LDA. PJM’s

     without regard to its proximity to the load it offsets, will not eliminate resource adequacy risk so
     much as convert generation-related constraints into transmission-related constraints. See PPL
     Protest at 20; ODEC asked for clarification on how locational resource adequacy would be
     impacted given that “[PJM] appears to allow a New Large Load in one zone to be supported by
     BYONC located in another zone.” See ODEC’s Protest at 9.

23   See IRAS Filing at 5–6.

24   September 23rd Answer at 38.



                                                 - 11 -
 assertion is simply wrong. The deliverability study does not obviate the need for the

CETO/CETL local resource adequacy study as the almost 20 year history of the locational

capacity market demonstrates.

       Allowing data centers to contract with generation outside a constrained region

reduces reliability for existing customers inside the constrained region. Under PJM’s IRAS

Filing, data center load could be contracted with capacity located outside the constrained

LDA that cannot meet the load in the constrained LDA and would not be subject to

curtailment. Higher load within the constrained region without offsetting generation within

the constrained region means there may be times when there is not enough capacity to

serve that load. PJM fails to state what load would be curtailed under those conditions.

       Ignoring locational issues simply shifts the costs and risks of resolving the

predictable consequences of meeting data center load to other customers.

       The fact that PJM ignores the fundamental locational element of the PJM Capacity

Market and all the resultant negative consequences means that the PJM IRAS Filing is not

just and reasonable.

              2. PJM Fails to Address Inconsistent Definitions of Qualifying Capacity

       The Market Monitor raised concerns regarding the proposed BYONC gating criteria

including the inconsistent definitions of capacity that can be used to satisfy the

requirements to meet the data center load in the IRAS Filing and the RBP Filing, the

proposed definition of new, allowing inferior capacity and shorter term capacity. 25

       In the September 23rd Answer, PJM fails to address any of the concerns raised by the

Market Monitor.

       PJM’s proposed BYONC gating criteria allow previously cleared capacity to count as

new and qualify as BYONC. PJM argues at 40 that “An advantage of PJM’s approach is that




25   See IMM Protest at 18–20.



                                            - 12 -
 Capacity Resources ready to participate in RPM and commit to provide capacity are not

disincentivized to do so while they wait for the BYONC marketplace to develop.” These

previously cleared resources are ready to commit and provide capacity because they were

already committed. While PJM states at 44 “Allowing existing Capacity Resources to

contract with New Large Loads would not solve the problem that the BYONC scheme is

designed to address,” the PJM IRAS Filing allows existing resources to be repackaged as

new. The IRAS Filing allows previously cleared resources to qualify as BYONC but would

not address the resource adequacy shortfall and would result in the shifting of risk and

costs to LSEs and their customers.

         PJM’s IRAS Filing violates the fundamental concept of BYONG that data centers

need to bring new capacity and not remove existing capacity from the capacity market and

cannibalize existing capacity resources. For that reason, the IRAS Filing is not just and

reasonable.

                 3. PJM Unjustly Shifts Generators’ ELCC Risk to Other Customers.

         PJM proposes to set a final and unchangeable ELCC value, and therefore a fixed

UCAP MW, for each BYONC arrangement at the level for which the BYONC first cleared. 26
27   The ELCC rating used to establish the initial UCAP value will be in place for up to 15

years. PJM responds (at 45) that recognizing changes in the actual ELCC values would

create uncertainty in the contractual arrangement and therefore undermine the incentive to

enter into such a contractual arrangement. Ignoring the uncertainty does not make it go

away. The IRAS Filing will shift the risk to customers. PJM misunderstands its role. PJM’s

role is not to create artificial incentives to allow the entry of data center load. If PJM




26     See IMM Protest at 20.

27     See IRAS Filing, Attachment A–(Marked Tariff), OATT Attachment DD-4 §§ VII(i)(i)–(ii).



                                                 - 13 -
 continues to believe in its flawed ELCC model it should not create arbitrary and

discriminatory exceptions to the ELCC rules.

       Under the IRAS Filing, the BYONC generators’ revenues will change with the ELCC

value. However, the IRAS Filing exempts the BYONC generator and the data center from

the risk of a reduced UCAP MW value and the requirement to make up any shortfall if the

ELCC decreases. Under the PJM rules, neither the capacity resource nor the data center load

has an obligation to cover the short position. This creates a reliability risk when the ELCC

decreases and the result is a capacity shortfall. The load of the data center in the BYONC

contract is no longer covered.

       If the ELCC decrease is significant, PJM will need to purchase additional capacity to

meet its reliability objective. Other PJM customers will pay for that additional capacity.

Other PJM customers will bear the risk and the associated costs.

       The fact that the IRAS Filing would arbitrarily freeze ELCC values and shift the risk

of actual ELCC changes to other customers makes the IRAS proposal unjust and

unreasonable.

                4. PJM Fails to Support the 50 MW Threshold.

       PJM did not respond to the Market Monitor’s demonstration that the proposed

definition could exclude significant amounts of data center load. Table 1 in the Market

Monitor’s Protest (at 31) shows that 28.5 percent of expected data center load is below the

50 MW threshold. Grouping by data center campus, 6.9 percent of expected data center

campus load is below the 50 MW threshold. It remains unclear how much of the data center

load would qualify as large load under PJM’s affiliate and one mile proximity rules. PJM

included the one mile rule to reduce the ability to game the rules by building a group of

smaller data centers. A more efficient and precise path to this end is to simply lower the

threshold.

       In addition to missing a significant level of data center load, PJM’s arbitrary

definition of large data center load is outdated. The rapid advancements in the data center


                                           - 14 -
 building technology mean that new data centers are going to be increasingly prefabricated

containerized computing units that can be built quickly and are scalable. 28 29 According to

market reports, small data centers that are typically 5 MW or less are expected to grow at a

higher rate than the larger data centers. 30 These data centers are considerably smaller than

the 50 MW threshold proposed by PJM.

               5. PJM’s One Mile Radius Criterion is Unworkable. and Unreasonable.

       The PJM IRAS Filing includes the following definition of Large Load:
               ‘Large Load’ shall mean end-use customer(s) load that has a
               cumulative peak load of 50 megawatts or greater at a single
               electrical site behind one or more points of interconnection, where
               for configurations involving multiple affiliated load facilities or
               multiple points of interconnection with affiliated load facilities
               behind them, all affiliated load facilities within a one-mile radius
               will be considered a single electrical site as further described in
               the PJM Manuals. 31

       PJM does not provide any details regarding the implementation of the one-mile

radius rule. PJM fails to explain or provide any criteria needed to uniformly and fairly

                  7. Interconnecting Large Data Center Loads Without Generation
                     Decreases Reliability and Increases Cost to Other Consumers.

       PJM makes the unsupported assertion that “calling for IRAS load reductions before

interconnecting new large loads without matching capacity and “protects native loads from

PJM system with curtailment provisions is the same as not adding large data center load or

adding data center load with matching generation. PJM provides no analytical support for

this claim. PJM’s operational history contradicts PJM’s claim. Higher levels of 8,760 hour

load in PJM without matching generation, net of accounting for curtailments, increases the

risk of unanticipated operational events. The higher the load, the larger the risk.

mean an increased frequency of maintenance outages and a higher risk of forced outages. 42

                8. PJM’s Proposal Will Negatively Affect Reliability.

       The essential requirement for scheduling planned outages is substantially lower load

during off peak seasons. Lower load outside peak summer and winter periods, typically

during the shoulder months, provides an opportunity to operate the grid reliably with less

available generation. PJM schedules planned maintenance outages during this period. As

the load without matching generation increases in PJM, PJM operations is and will be

challenged to meet higher loads with lower generation capacity due to planned outages.

PJM acknowledged this important concern. During the Critical Issue Fast Path Education,

PJM stated that “if load continues to increase 8,760 hours/year, and the BRA clears the IRM,

either: Future generation outages may be denied/deferred to the following season to avoid

emergency procedures; Not a good option - Units may then be less reliable or become an

Unplanned Outages if Planned/Maintenance Outages requests are denied.” 45

       In addition to the scheduling of outages, when units reach their emission limits they

are no longer available to meet 8,760 hour load. There are multiple generating units in PJM

today that are subject to emission restrictions. 46 In some cases, the restrictions limit the total

output within a rolling calendar year to only a few hours. There are other restrictions that

have not been previously binding that have become binding and more will become binding

as unit capacity factors increase. These emission restrictions are not considered in the

resource adequacy models and capacity accreditation. Under PJM’s ELCC based
